strengths: Principled and well-motivated statistical framework: The paper identifies a fundamental issue in the current LLM-as-a-judge paradigm—namely, that pooling heterogeneous LLM judges uniformly is statistically misspecified and yields biased rankings and invalid uncertainty quantification.

Rigorous theoretical development: The paper establishes non-trivial identifiability conditions (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3) under natural location and scale normalizations, and derives consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE (Theorem 3.4) enabling valid Wald confidence intervals.

Convincing simulation results: The simulation experiments clearly validate the theoretical O(1/T) convergence rate and demonstrate that the proposed estimator maintains nominal 95% coverage, whereas the misspecified unweighted BTL suffers from severe under-coverage as the number of comparisons grows.

Solid empirical validation: Evaluated across multiple benchmarks (MT-Bench, UltraFeedback, Chatbot Arena) and a 45-model panel, showing superior sample efficiency and closer alignment to human judgment rankings (e.g., Spearman rho of 0.9955 vs. 0.9699 on Chatbot Arena).
weaknesses: Simplified judge error model: The framework models judge heterogeneity solely through a single scalar discrimination parameter gamma_k. It does not account for well-known LLM judge pathologies such as position bias, verbosity bias, or self-enhancement bias (judges preferring their own outputs when evaluator and candidate sets overlap).

Assumption of task-invariant judge reliability: Judge discrimination gamma_k is assumed constant across all comparison items, ignoring the reality that LLM judges exhibit domain- and topic-specific proficiencies (e.g., strong in coding or math vs. humanities).

Ad-hoc handling of ties: The paper handles ties by assigning y = 0.5 into the binary cross-entropy loss rather than incorporating a formal tie mechanism (such as the Rao-Kupper or Davidson extensions of the Bradley-Terry model).

Limited comparison with specialized baselines: Empirical comparisons in the main text are primarily restricted to unweighted BTL, omitting head-to-head empirical comparisons against related crowdsourcing/ranking methods mentioned in the literature (e.g., Crowd-BT, FTR/GTR, or IRT aggregation methods).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely, important, and practical problem in the LLM-as-a-judge evaluation ecosystem: LLM judges vary substantially in reliability, and uniform aggregation under the standard Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model is misspecified, leading to biased rankings and overconfident/invalid confidence intervals.

The theoretical foundation is clean and well-developed: the authors establish parameter identifiability under natural normalization constraints (mean zero for scores, geometric mean one for judge discrimination parameters) and prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE, enabling valid Wald confidence intervals.

The simulation studies in Section 4 are rigorous and informative, convincingly validating the theoretical O(1/T) convergence rate and demonstrating that the judge-aware model maintains nominal 95% coverage while the unweighted baseline exhibits severe under-coverage as sample size grows.

Empirical evaluation spans multiple realistic settings (MT-Bench, UltraFeedback, Chatbot Arena, and an in-house dataset with 18 LLM judges), showing improved data efficiency, tighter confidence intervals, and higher Spearman correlation with human judgments compared to unweighted aggregation.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly organized, and transparent about its assumptions and modeling choices.
weaknesses: The statistical novelty is somewhat modest: introducing multiplicative discrimination parameters in logistic paired-comparison models is standard in Item Response Theory (IRT) and psychometrics (e.g., two-parameter logistic models, Otani et al., 2016). While the adaptation to reference-free LLM-as-a-judge aggregation with formal inference is valuable, the core model extension is relatively incremental.

The theoretical asymptotic guarantees in Section 3.3 strictly assume uniform i.i.d. sampling over all triples (i, j, k). In real-world LLM evaluation environments (such as Chatbot Arena or active evaluation pipelines), comparison graphs are typically sparse, non-uniform, and adaptive.

The model only captures scalar judge discriminability (gamma_k), but LLM judges frequently suffer from systematic directional biases (e.g., position/order bias, response length bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias), which are not accounted for in this framework.

The handling of ties in Section 5.1 (assigning y = 0.5 into the binary cross-entropy loss) is an ad-hoc heuristic that deviates from the generative binary statistical model analyzed in Section 3. Incorporating principled tie models (such as Davidson or Rao-Kupper extensions to BTL) would make the theoretical-empirical connection tighter.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and critical practical issue in LLM evaluation: the substantial variation in LLM judge reliability and the statistical misspecification of pooling heterogeneous judges uniformly.

The proposed judge-aware BTL model is conceptually clean and intuitive, capturing annotator discriminability through multiplicative scale parameters rather than simple label-flipping honesty parameters.

The theoretical characterization of identifiability (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3) and large-sample properties (Theorem 3.4) provides a rigorous statistical foundation for constructing Wald confidence intervals on model scores and differences.

The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and the simulation experiments thoroughly validate the theoretical asymptotic convergence rates and Wald interval coverage under the proposed data-generating process.
weaknesses: Lack of competitive baselines: Despite surveying related ranking and weighting methods in Section 2 (such as GTR/FTR by Dhurandhar et al., REM by Yang et al., and Crowd-BT by Chen et al.), the empirical evaluation compares solely against the standard unweighted BTL model. Demonstrating clear advantages over existing weighted or reputation-based ranking methods is essential.

Flawed efficiency evaluation metric in Section 5.3: In the subsampling study, the weighted model's subsampled estimates are evaluated by Pearson correlation against its own full-data estimate (s_w vs. s_w^ref), while the unweighted model is correlated against its own full-data estimate (s_u vs. s_u^ref). This measures self-consistency and internal stability rather than actual ranking accuracy or recovery of true model capabilities.

Ad-hoc handling of ties: Ties in real-world evaluations are handled by setting y = 0.5 in the binary cross-entropy loss. While common in practice, this violates the underlying Bernoulli likelihood model, which formally invalidates the asymptotic Fisher information and the nominal coverage guarantees of the resulting Wald confidence intervals. A principled extension (e.g., Davidson or Rao-Kupper models for ties) would be statistically sounder.

Ignoring judge-specific systematic biases: Real LLM judges are well documented to suffer from severe systematic biases (e.g., position bias, length/verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias). Modeling judge reliability purely as a discrimination multiplier gamma_k without intercept or bias terms can conflate judge bias with low discriminability or distort the score estimates when judges evaluate their own model family.

Gap between theoretical assumptions and benchmark topology: The asymptotic normality theory assumes uniform i.i.d. sampling of triples across all candidate pairs and judges. In practice (such as Chatbot Arena or crowd/LLM platforms), comparison graphs are highly non-uniform and sparse, leaving the theoretical guarantees somewhat disconnected from practical settings.

strengths: Principled and timely framework: The paper tackles an important and increasingly prominent practical issue in LLM evaluation—heterogeneity in judge quality within LLM-as-a-judge pipelines—providing a statistically principled extension to the Bradley–Terry–Luce (BTL) model.

Rigorous statistical theory: The paper establishes formal identifiability conditions (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3) under natural centering and geometric-mean constraints, and provides a thorough asymptotic normality and consistency proof (Theorem 3.4) enabling valid Wald confidence intervals.

Well-designed simulation validation: The synthetic experiments clearly demonstrate the theoretical O(1/T) convergence rate and convincingly show that the judge-aware model maintains nominal 95% coverage, whereas misspecified unweighted BTL suffers severe under-coverage as sample size grows.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated on multiple public benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback) and a newly collected 36K-comparison dataset spanning 45 models and 18 LLM judges. The estimated discrimination parameters γ align with intuitive model quality differences (down-weighting noisy judges) and improve rank alignment with human preferences.
weaknesses: Optimization gap vs. theoretical guarantees: The joint log-likelihood over model scores s and log-scales α is non-convex. While Theorem 3.4 provides asymptotic properties for the global MLE, the actual algorithm is projected Adam, which only guarantees convergence to stationary points. A discussion of optimization landscapes, sensitivity to random initializations, or potential local optima is missing.

Conditional independence assumption across LLM judges: The framework assumes that judges' evaluations are conditionally independent given model qualities and judge scales. In reality, LLM judges often share training corpora, base architectures, or common failure modes (e.g., verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias). Correlated errors among judges could lead to overconfident standard error estimates and narrow confidence intervals in practice.

Limited empirical comparison against other weighted/reliability baselines: The main experimental comparisons primarily benchmark against the standard unweighted BTL model. Although methods like Crowd-BT (Chen et al., 2013) or FTR (Dhurandhar et al., 2024) are discussed in Related Work, including quantitative comparisons with these alternative weighting/annotator-modeling baselines on the benchmark datasets would have further strengthened the empirical claims.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: Addressing evaluator heterogeneity in the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm is essential, as treating all LLM judges as equally reliable leads to statistically misspecified aggregation, biased leaderboards, and artificially overconfident uncertainty estimates.

Principled statistical formulation: The judge-aware BTL model introduces multiplicative judge discrimination parameters in a clean and interpretable manner. Identifiability is rigorously established under minimal conditions (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3), fixing location and scale naturally.

Solid theoretical guarantees: The paper provides complete proofs for consistency and asymptotic normality of the MLE under an unconstrained reparameterization (Theorem 3.4), enabling valid Wald confidence intervals for latent model scores and judge reliabilities.

Thorough empirical evaluation and simulations: The synthetic experiments clearly validate the theoretical O(1/T) convergence rate and demonstrate that standard BTL suffers from severe under-coverage under misspecification, while the proposed model maintains nominal coverage with narrower intervals. Real-world evaluation spanning MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and an in-house dataset with 45 models shows consistent alignment with human preferences and improved data efficiency.

Valuable practical insights and extensions: The unsupervised estimation accurately identifies known high- and low-quality judges (e.g., Table 2). Additionally, Appendix F.6 nicely extends the theory to covariate-dependent (length-augmented) judge discriminability with an accompanying identifiability proof.
weaknesses: Idealized theoretical design assumptions: Theorem 3.4 and Corollary A.7 rely on an i.i.d. full-support random design with fixed (N, K) where every triple (i, j, k) has positive sampling probability. In realistic evaluation settings, the comparison graph is often sparse and comparison allocations are non-uniform or adaptive. While Appendix F.7 empirically evaluates connected sparse graphs, the theoretical results do not cover the growing (N, K) or sparse graph regime.

Conditionally independent error assumption: The model assumes that judge decisions are conditionally independent given latent scores and discrimination parameters. In practice, LLM evaluators often share systemic correlated biases (e.g., length/verbosity bias, formatting preference, or self-enhancement bias toward their own model family) that cannot be fully captured by a single scalar discrimination parameter.

Lack of empirical comparison to psychometric / crowdsourcing baselines: The empirical comparison is predominantly between the proposed judge-aware model and unweighted BTL. Including quantitative comparisons against established crowdsourcing/IRT pairwise models (e.g., Crowd-BT or Bayesian IRT extensions) on the benchmark tasks would strengthen the empirical claims.

Sensitivity to near-zero discrimination: As noted in Section 5.3 and Appendix F.3, judges with estimated discrimination near zero (gamma ~ 0) cause numerical instability in Fisher information inversion for confidence intervals, requiring ad-hoc post-hoc exclusion. Incorporating a slight regularization or prior over judge parameters would make the framework more robust out-of-the-box.

strengths: Principled statistical formulation: The paper tackles a well-documented and timely problem in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation—heterogeneity in judge reliability—by extending the Bradley–Terry–Luce (BTL) model with judge-specific discrimination parameters ($\gamma_k$). This provides a probabilistic interpretation that naturally downweights uninformative or noisy evaluators.

Theoretical soundness: The manuscript provides clean identifiability results (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3) under the zero-sum and geometric-mean normalization constraints, along with consistency and asymptotic normality results (Theorem 3.4) that justify Wald confidence intervals for latent model scores and pairwise differences.

Comprehensive validation: The empirical evaluation is thorough, featuring controlled simulation experiments (validating the $O(1/T)$ rate and confirming that unweighted BTL suffers severe under-coverage due to misspecification) and multiple real-world benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback), supplemented by a newly collected dataset of 36K comparisons across 45 candidate models and 18 LLM judges.

Clear presentation and robust appendices: The paper is well-written, cleanly structured, and supported by extensive supplementary material, including complete asymptotic proofs, algorithmic details (Projected Adam), sensitivity analyses to tie-handling, and covariate extensions (e.g., question length).
weaknesses: Conceptual and algorithmic originality: The proposed formulation $P(Y=1) = \sigma(\gamma_k(s_i - s_j))$ is essentially the two-parameter logistic (2PL) Item Response Theory (IRT) formulation adapted to pairwise comparisons without a fixed reference. While its application to LLM judges is timely, the underlying modeling framework is well-established in psychometrics and crowdsourced aggregation.

Asymptotic framework assumptions: Theorem 3.4 operates under classical fixed $(N, K)$ asymptotics as $T \to \infty$ with an i.i.d. full-support design ($\pi_{ijk} \ge \pi_{\min} > 0$). In many practical LLM evaluation pipelines, $N$ (number of candidate models) can be comparable to or grow with the number of comparisons, and comparison graphs can be sparse. The theoretical analysis does not cover modern high-dimensional or sparse comparison regimes.

Simplified error structure: The model assumes that judge discrepancies are captured entirely by a scalar sensitivity parameter $\gamma_k$ under conditional independence. In practice, LLM judges frequently share systemic biases (such as self-preference/family bias, verbosity bias, or correlated errors due to overlapping pretraining data) that cannot be fully captured by a single discriminability scale.

Modest differences on curated benchmark settings: In datasets where judges are relatively capable (such as MT-Bench in Table 1), the model rankings are largely identical between the unweighted and judge-aware models. The most substantial gains appear in synthetic or artificially mixed-quality judge panels (e.g., Section 5.4), indicating that the practical impact may be modest when evaluation is already conducted using well-curated LLM judges.
